title: Breathless after a mountain bike fall
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 20-year-old man brought to the ED by ambulance after falling onto his left side while mountain biking, now breathless with left pleuritic chest pain and deteriorating. The candidate must recognise a tension pneumothorax clinically and call for decompression without waiting for imaging. They then interpret his observations, bloods with a venous gas and the chest X-ray, justify the diagnosis against the differentials (cardiac tamponade, haemothorax, rib fractures, asthma, PE), and outline ED management and safety netting.
focus: Breathlessness after blunt chest trauma: recognising tension pneumothorax as a clinical diagnosis, decompressing before imaging, and reading the chest X-ray
stem: You are the intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Bob Dane, a 20-year-old man, has been brought in by ambulance after falling off his bike while mountain biking. He is short of breath. He is in an acute bay on a cardiac monitor with an IV cannula in place. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. Bloods and a venous blood gas have been sent, and a chest X-ray was taken soon after he arrived.
tasks: Take a focused history from Bob and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. He is breathless, so keep your questions targeted (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, blood results with a venous gas, and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Bob Dane, a 20-year-old arts student. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are sitting up on the trolley, breathing fast and shallow, holding your left side. You can speak only short sentences and stop to catch your breath. You are frightened. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Bob came in by ambulance about 20 minutes ago after a fall from his mountain bike. At triage his resp rate was 26, sats 93% on room air, heart rate 116, BP 118 over 72, temp 36.6, pain 6 out of 10. He's on the monitor, the cannula is in, bloods and a venous gas have gone, and the radiographer did a chest X-ray about 15 minutes ago. It hasn't been reported yet. He's looking worse, so I've just repeated his obs: resp rate 28, sats 91% on room air, heart rate 134, BP 88 over 60. He's not on any oxygen. What would you like?"

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask for high-flow oxygen by mask, the nurse puts it on. Your sats come up to about 94%, but you are still just as breathless and your BP stays low.
  • If they call the senior ED doctor or the trauma team, the nurse says: "I've called them. They're coming now."
  • If they say this is a tension pneumothorax and ask for immediate decompression, the nurse says: "The senior doctor is on the way with the decompression kit. Keep going." The examiner notes it, and nothing else changes in Part 1.
  • If they say they will decompress the chest themselves, or ask for an eFAST, the nurse says: "The senior doctor is arriving with the kit and the ultrasound now. Keep going." Credit item 18 as for a request for decompression.
  • If they keep you sitting up, you say: "Don't lie me down, it's worse flat."
  • If they do nothing about your breathing in the first few minutes, the nurse says: "He's looking greyer and more breathless and his BP is still low. Do you want to do something?" You become harder to understand.
  • If they ask for the X-ray or blood results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "I just can't catch my breath."

About a minute in, between breaths, whatever you are being asked, say: "Am I going to die?" If they answer calmly and honestly, you settle a little. If they ignore it, look more frightened.

History (give only when asked; short phrases):

The breathlessness and the fall

  • Onset: it started about 1 hour ago, just after you fell off your bike, and it has been getting worse since.
  • The fall: you were mountain biking on a rocky downhill track, lost control and fell badly onto your left side. Your riding friend called the ambulance. You noticed the breathlessness straight after the fall.
  • Head and neck (only if asked): you were wearing a helmet. You did not hit your head, did not black out and remember everything. No neck pain.
  • Other injuries (only if asked): grazes on your left arm and thigh. No tummy pain and no pain at the tip of your shoulder. You can move your arms and legs normally.

The chest pain ("My chest hurts a bit too.")

  • Site: the left side of your chest. It does not spread anywhere.
  • Character: sharp.
  • Worse with: breathing in. It also hurts to move, and the left side is sore when pressed.
  • Onset: straight after the fall.

Other symptoms (only if asked)

  • Your heart is racing. You have not fainted or nearly fainted.
  • The pain is not crushing or heavy, does not go to your arm, neck, jaw or back, and is not tearing. It is not eased by leaning forward. No sweating or nausea before the fall.
  • No cough, no phlegm, no coughing up blood. No fever, no recent cold or flu.
  • No wheeze. This does not feel like the asthma you had as a child.
  • No calf pain or leg swelling, no recent long trips or operations, no previous clots.
  • You have never had a collapsed lung before.

Past medical history

  • Asthma as a child. No flare-ups for years, never in hospital for it.
  • Appendix removed 6 years ago.
  • No heart or other lung problems.
  • Last tetanus shot: at school, not sure when (only if asked).

Medications: a Ventolin puffer, which you have not used for years. Nothing else, no over-the-counter medicines.

Allergies: none.

Last ate or drank (only if asked): a sandwich about 2 hours ago.

Family history: your parents and younger brother are well. No one in the family has had a collapsed lung (only if asked).

Social history

  • You have never smoked or vaped. No recreational drugs.
  • Alcohol: 1 or 2 drinks on Friday and Saturday.
  • You study arts at university and work part-time in a café.
  • Very active: you run 3 times a week, mountain bike every week and play football.
  • You have a girlfriend, and your friends and family live nearby.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think you might have broken a rib, but you have never felt this breathless and you are scared you are going to die. You want to be able to breathe and you want your parents called.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: obviously breathless and distressed, sitting upright, using his neck and shoulder muscles to breathe. Speaking in short sentences. Not cyanosed. No supplemental oxygen (unless the candidate has asked for it). Weight about 72 kg, athletic build.
  • Vital signs: HR 134, BP 88/60, RR 28, SpO2 91% on room air (or 94% if oxygen has been given). Temperature 36.6 °C.
  • Hands and peripheries: cool, capillary refill 3 seconds. Radial pulse fast, regular and weak.
  • Neck: neck veins distended. Trachea deviated to the right.
  • Heart: heart sounds present and not muffled, no murmur, no rub.
  • Chest wall: bruising and an abrasion over the left lateral chest. Tender over the left lateral ribs. No crepitus, no surgical emphysema, no flail segment, no open wound.
  • Respiratory: reduced expansion on the left. Hyper-resonant to percussion over the left chest. Breath sounds reduced over the whole left lung. Right lung: normal expansion, resonant, vesicular breath sounds, no added sounds. No wheeze.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender, including the left upper quadrant. No guarding. Appendicectomy scar.
  • Neurological: alert, GCS 15, no cervical spine tenderness.
  • Legs: grazes on the left thigh. Calves soft and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Bob's identity and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Recognises an unwell, deteriorating patient from the nurse's observations and his appearance, and acts early: asks for high-flow oxygen, calls the senior ED doctor or trauma team, keeps him sitting up, and then keeps questions short and closed.
check.d: Credit when oxygen is requested and senior help is called within the first few minutes.

check.x: Explains to Bob in plain words what is happening (air has leaked around the lung and is pressing on the lung and heart; a needle and then a tube will let it out) and answers 'Am I going to die?' honestly and calmly.
History
Characterises the breathlessness, the chest pain and the injury:
check.d: Credit when the timing after the fall, the mechanism and the pleuritic left-sided pain are all elicited.

kids.x: Onset 1 hour ago, straight after the fall, and getting worse
Mechanism: fell badly onto his left side on a rocky downhill track
Pain: left-sided, sharp, worse on breathing in, no radiation
Pain worse on moving and when the left side is pressed (rib injury)

check.x: Asks about features of the differentials:
check.d: Credit when at least 3 differentials are screened in short closed questions.

kids.x: Haemodynamic symptoms: palpitations, presyncope or syncope (heart racing, no fainting)
ACS and aortic dissection: crushing pain, radiation to the arm, neck or jaw, tearing pain to the back, sweating (none)
PE: leg pain or swelling, immobility, travel, previous clots, haemoptysis (none)
Pneumonia: cough, sputum, fever, recent illness (none)
Asthma: wheeze, previous asthma (childhood only, no flare for years)
Pericarditis: pain eased by leaning forward, recent viral illness (none)

check.x: Screens for other injuries from the fall: helmet, head strike and loss of consciousness, neck pain, abdominal or left shoulder-tip pain (spleen), and limb injuries.
Takes the past medical history: childhood asthma with no flare for years, appendicectomy 6 years ago, no previous collapsed lung.
Takes the medication history (Ventolin, not used for years) and asks about allergies (none) before giving analgesia.
Takes an AMPLE-focused history: last ate or drank (a sandwich about 2 hours ago), smoking (never), alcohol and drugs (1–2 drinks at weekends, no drugs); brief family history.
check.d: Credit when last meal, smoking and alcohol are asked about.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks he broke a rib, fears dying, wants to breathe and his parents called.
Examination
General inspection: distress, accessory muscle use, speech, cyanosis and whether he is on oxygen (he is not).
Cardiovascular examination: pulse rate and volume, BP, peripheral perfusion, distended neck veins, and heart sounds (not muffled).
Respiratory examination identifying the left-sided signs:
check.d: Credit when the tracheal deviation and at least 2 of the other 3 are found.

kids.x: Reduced breath sounds over the left lung, with a normal right lung

check.x: Examines the chest wall and for other injuries: left lateral tenderness and bruising, no surgical emphysema, flail segment or open wound; abdomen including the left upper quadrant; GCS and cervical spine.
States during Part 1 that this is a left tension pneumothorax, a clinical diagnosis, and asks for immediate decompression without waiting for the X-ray.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: worsening since triage (RR and SpO2 yellow then); now a red-zone systolic BP of 88 with HR 134, RR 28 and SpO2 91% yellow; in shock and needs a senior doctor at the bedside now.
Reads the chest X-ray systematically:
check.d: Credit when the complete left lung collapse and the mediastinal shift are both named.

kids.x: Confirms correct patient and film and comments on adequacy (one phrase)
Complete collapse of the left lung, with no lung markings in the left hemithorax
Trachea, heart and mediastinum shifted to the right
Hyperexpanded left hemithorax: depressed, flattened left hemidiaphragm and widened intercostal spaces
No rib fracture seen, no effusion, right lung clear, no cardiomegaly

check.x: States that the X-ray confirms the diagnosis, but tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and imaging must never delay decompression.

Interprets the bloods and venous gas: normal Hb (no evidence yet of major blood loss, though an early Hb is unreliable), normal coagulation (reassuring for the intercostal catheter, which would not be delayed for results), mildly raised lactate (hypoperfusion), and a neutrophilia from stress.

Gives the diagnosis as left tension pneumothorax after blunt chest trauma, with obstructive shock, justified by the history (fall onto the left side, breathlessness, pleuritic pain), the signs (tracheal deviation, hyper-resonance, reduced breath sounds, distended neck veins) and the observations (tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia).
check.d: Credit when at least 3 supporting features are given, including a history feature and a clinical sign.

check.x: Names the differentials with a feature against each: cardiac tamponade (heart sounds not muffled, trachea deviated, hyper-resonance), haemothorax (hyper-resonant rather than dull, no effusion on X-ray), rib fractures (do not explain the shift or shock), asthma or PE (one-sided signs after trauma).
check.d: Credit when at least 3 are named, including tamponade.

check.x: Management
Escalates: resus bay, senior ED doctor and trauma team at the bedside now, ABCDE primary survey, continuous monitoring.
Gives high-flow oxygen, 15 L/min by non-rebreather mask.

Decompresses the left chest immediately: needle decompression at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, or the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line (or finger thoracostomy by a trained clinician), then reassesses.
check.d: Credit for either needle site or finger thoracostomy on the correct (left) side.

check.x: Follows with a left intercostal catheter in the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the safe triangle, inserted aseptically and connected to an underwater seal drain, with a repeat chest X-ray to check the tube position and lung re-expansion.

Gives analgesia: titrated IV opioid in small increments with care given hypotension (e.g. fentanyl 0.5 microgram/kg, about 25–50 microgram, repeated to effect), plus regular paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly (max 4 g/day).

Completes the trauma work-up and disposition: secondary survey, eFAST (haemothorax, pericardial fluid, spleen), ECG, group and hold; wound care and tetanus status (give tetanus vaccine ± immunoglobulin per the Australian Immunisation Handbook); admits under the trauma or surgical team.
Safety netting
Tells Bob in plain words to call 000 or come straight back to the ED for sudden or worsening breathlessness, new or worse chest pain, or feeling faint.

Gives activity advice: no flying until a follow-up X-ray confirms full resolution and then for about 2 more weeks (confirm with the treating team); no mountain biking or football until cleared; before any scuba diving, a diving medical assessment with a SPUMS-trained doctor.
check.d: Credit when flying and contact sport or mountain biking are covered.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: clinic review with a repeat chest X-ray (respiratory or trauma clinic) and a discharge letter to his GP.
Answers Bob's recurrence question: low risk after a healed traumatic pneumothorax, unlike a spontaneous one; not smoking or vaping lowers the risk further.

part2.lead: Here are his observations, his blood results with the venous gas, and the chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Ask these only after the examiner reads question 4, one at a time:

  • "When can I get back on my bike and play footy?"
  • "Could this happen again?"

You are relieved you are not going to die. If the candidate explains clearly, you agree to the plan. If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets on room air, before any treatment in the ED.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage (09:40) RR 26 and SpO2 93% on room air are in the yellow zone; HR 116, BP 118/72 and temperature 36.6 °C are white. At 10:00 systolic BP 88 is in the red zone, with HR 134, RR 28 and SpO2 91% in the yellow zone. CRT has lengthened to 3 seconds, pain is 7/10 and distress severe.
  • Meaning: rapid deterioration over 20 minutes into shock (shock index about 1.5) with hypoxia. Together with distended neck veins and tracheal deviation, this is obstructive shock from a tension pneumothorax, not hypovolaemia.
  • Changes: the yellow zone at triage called for a clinical review. The red zone now calls for a rapid response: in the ED, the senior ED doctor and trauma team at the bedside now, high-flow oxygen and immediate decompression.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: acute bay, monitor on, IV cannula, bloods and VBG sent, CXR requested
Repeat set at medical review: more breathless; doctor at bedside

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.result: Venous sample collected at 09:45 on cannulation, on room air. Group and hold: group O positive, antibody screen negative; sample held for crossmatch.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 148 and platelets normal. WCC 12.8 with neutrophils 10.2. Electrolytes, urea and creatinine normal. INR, APTT and fibrinogen normal. Venous pH 7.36, pCO2 44 and bicarbonate 24 are normal; lactate 2.6 is mildly raised. Group and hold done.
  • Meaning: no laboratory evidence yet of major bleeding, but an early Hb does not exclude haemorrhage. The neutrophilia is a stress response, not infection. The lactate shows early hypoperfusion. A venous gas says nothing about oxygenation.
  • Changes: normal coagulation is reassuring for the intercostal catheter, which would not be delayed for results. The group and hold allows blood if a haemothorax appears. Repeat the lactate after decompression.

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Patient: Bob Dane, DOB 01/07/2006.

Examination: chest X-ray, AP erect (mobile, sitting), taken today at 09:48.

Clinical details: 20-year-old man, fall from a mountain bike onto the left side. Left pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath.

Technical: AP projection, not rotated, adequate inspiration and exposure.

Findings:

  • Lines and devices: ECG electrodes only.
  • Airway: trachea deviated to the right.
  • Left lung: the entire left lung is collapsed towards the hilum, with a visible visceral pleural edge. No lung markings in the rest of the left hemithorax, which is lucent and hyperexpanded.
  • Right lung: clear. No consolidation or pneumothorax.
  • Pleura: no pleural effusion or fluid level on either side.
  • Diaphragm: left hemidiaphragm depressed and flattened, with widened left intercostal spaces. Right hemidiaphragm normal.
  • Heart and mediastinum: the heart and mediastinum are shifted to the right. Heart size cannot be reliably assessed on an AP film; no obvious cardiomegaly. No pneumomediastinum.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no displaced rib fracture is seen. No surgical emphysema.

Conclusion: large left pneumothorax with complete collapse of the left lung, a depressed left hemidiaphragm and shift of the trachea and mediastinum to the right, in keeping with tension pneumothorax in this clinical context. No effusion to suggest haemothorax. No rib fracture seen. Findings phoned to the ED.
handover.model:
• Read: correct patient, AP erect mobile film taken today at 09:48, technically adequate. Complete collapse of the left lung with no lung markings beyond the visceral pleural edge. Trachea, heart and mediastinum shifted to the right. Hyperexpanded left hemithorax with a depressed, flattened left hemidiaphragm and widened intercostal spaces. Right lung clear, no cardiomegaly (heart size is hard to judge on an AP film), no effusion or fluid level, no rib fracture seen.
  • Meaning: a large left pneumothorax under tension, matching the clinical signs. There is no haemothorax on the film. An X-ray can miss a rib fracture, so the left lateral tenderness still counts as a rib injury.
  • Changes: the film confirms what was already a clinical diagnosis. Decompression should never wait for imaging. Decompress now, then insert an intercostal catheter and repeat the film to check the tube position and re-expansion.

ask: The ED registrar has just arrived at the bedside. Please give an ISBAR handover of Bob Dane, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Bob now, here in the emergency department.
Bob's chest drain is removed a few days later and he is ready to go home. What would you tell him, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Bob Dane, 20.
  • Situation: left tension pneumothorax with obstructive shock; BP 88/60 (red zone: rapid response), HR 134, RR 28, SpO2 91% RA (yellow); at triage RR 26 and SpO2 93% were already yellow, so he has worsened over 20 minutes into shock.
  • Background: fell onto his left side mountain biking 1 hour ago; breathlessness and sharp left pleuritic pain since; childhood asthma, appendicectomy, never smoked, no allergies.
  • Assessment: correct patient, adequate AP erect film: complete left lung collapse, mediastinal shift right, depressed left hemidiaphragm, no effusion or rib fracture, right lung clear, no obvious cardiomegaly; matches trachea deviated right, distended neck veins, left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds. Hb 148 normal (an early Hb does not exclude bleeding), coagulation normal, neutrophilia from stress, lactate 2.6 (hypoperfusion).
  • Recommendation: please decompress the left chest now, then an intercostal catheter; trauma team called.

Left tension pneumothorax after blunt chest trauma, with obstructive shock: fall onto the left side, immediate breathlessness, sharp pleuritic pain; trachea deviated right, hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds on the left, distended neck veins; tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia; CXR confirms. It is a clinical diagnosis.

  • Cardiac tamponade: for: trauma, distended neck veins, hypotension; against: heart sounds not muffled, trachea deviated, hyper-resonance.
  • Haemothorax or haemopneumothorax: for: blunt trauma, shock; against: hyper-resonant not dull, no effusion, Hb normal.
  • Rib fractures: for: left lateral tenderness, pain on moving; against: cannot explain the shift or shock.
  • Asthma or PE: against: no wheeze or clot risk factors; one-sided signs after trauma.

1. Resus bay; senior ED doctor and trauma team now; ABCDE primary survey; continuous monitoring.
  2. High-flow oxygen, 15 L/min by non-rebreather mask.
  3. Immediate left decompression, no further imaging: needle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, or the 2nd space mid-clavicular line, or finger thoracostomy; reassess.
  4. Intercostal catheter in the left 4th or 5th space in the safe triangle, aseptic, underwater seal drain (normal coagulation is reassuring, but the drain is not delayed for results); repeat CXR for position and re-expansion.
  5. Titrated IV opioid in small increments with care given hypotension (e.g. fentanyl 0.5 microgram/kg, about 25–50 microgram, repeated to effect), plus regular paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly (max 4 g/day).
  6. Secondary survey, eFAST, ECG; group and hold done; wound care and tetanus status (give tetanus vaccine ± immunoglobulin per the Australian Immunisation Handbook).
  7. Admit under the trauma or surgical team.

• Plain words: the fall let air leak around the lung, which collapsed and pressed on the heart; the drain let it out and the lung has re-expanded.
  • Red flags (000 or ED): sudden or worsening breathlessness, new or worse chest pain, feeling faint.
  • Activity: no flying until a follow-up X-ray confirms full resolution and then for about 2 more weeks (confirm with the treating team); no mountain biking or football until cleared; before any scuba diving, a diving medical assessment with a SPUMS-trained doctor.
  • Recurrence: a traumatic pneumothorax that has fully healed has a low recurrence risk, unlike a spontaneous one; not smoking or vaping lowers the risk further.
  • Follow-up: clinic review with a repeat chest X-ray; letter to his GP.

ddx.dx: Left tension pneumothorax after blunt chest trauma, with obstructive shock
ddx.for: Breathlessness and sharp left pleuritic pain straight after a fall onto the left side, with tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins, left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds, tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, and complete left lung collapse with mediastinal shift on X-ray.

ddx.dx: Cardiac tamponade from blunt cardiac injury
ddx.for: Chest trauma with distended neck veins, tachycardia and hypotension.
ddx.against: Heart sounds are not muffled, the trachea is deviated, and the left chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds on one side; a normal cardiac silhouette does not exclude acute tamponade, so eFAST is still needed.

ddx.for: Blunt left chest trauma with shock and reduced left breath sounds.
ddx.against: The left chest is hyper-resonant rather than dull, the X-ray shows no effusion or fluid level, the neck veins are distended rather than flat, and the Hb is normal.

ddx.dx: Left rib fractures with pulmonary contusion
ddx.for: Left lateral chest tenderness and bruising, with pain that is worse on moving and breathing.
ddx.against: Rib fractures alone cannot explain the tracheal deviation, hyper-resonance or shock, and no fracture is seen on X-ray.

ddx.for: Childhood asthma, a Ventolin puffer, and acute breathlessness.
ddx.against: No flare for years, no wheeze, one-sided signs, and onset straight after trauma.

ddx.for: Sudden breathlessness with pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia.
ddx.against: No leg swelling, immobility, travel or previous clots, and the trauma and one-sided signs explain the picture.

guide:
In Part 1, the nurse gives both sets of observations at the start. Bob is breathless and answers in short phrases. He asks "Am I going to die?" about a minute in. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they examine. A good candidate acts on the observations early (high-flow oxygen, senior help) and, once they have examined the chest, says this is a tension pneumothorax and asks for immediate decompression. When they do, the nurse says the senior doctor is coming with the kit and the candidate carries on. Credit item 18 only if they ask for decompression without waiting for the X-ray. If the candidate asks for the X-ray or bloods in Part 1, say these will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Bob asks his questions after question 4 is read.

A high-performing candidate links the breathlessness to the fall, characterises the pleuritic left-sided pain, and quickly screens for ACS, dissection, PE, pneumonia and asthma, and for other injuries. They find the tracheal deviation, distended neck veins, left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds, name tension pneumothorax in Part 1 and ask for decompression before any imaging. In Part 2 they read the X-ray systematically, including the mediastinal shift and the depressed left hemidiaphragm. They state that the film should never have been needed to make the diagnosis, separate tension from tamponade and haemothorax at the bedside, and give the correct decompression sites, then an intercostal catheter in the safe triangle.

A borderline candidate takes a generic breathlessness history, misses the tracheal deviation or the neck veins, and waits for the X-ray before acting. They may call it a simple pneumothorax or rib fractures, confuse it with tamponade, or give the wrong side or site for decompression. Waiting for imaging in a hypotensive patient with these signs, or giving no oxygen and calling no help, is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: left tension pneumothorax after blunt chest trauma

A pneumothorax is air in the pleural space. Bob fell onto his left side and became breathless straight away, with sharp left pleuritic pain. Within an hour he had tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins, left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds, with tachycardia, hypotension and hypoxia. That is a tension pneumothorax. A one-way valve lets air into the pleural space with each breath but not out. The ipsilateral lung collapses, the mediastinum is pushed to the other side, and the venae cavae are compressed. Venous return falls, causing obstructive shock. It can kill quickly, and it is treated as soon as it is recognised.

Types of pneumothorax

  • Primary spontaneous: rupture of apical blebs in people without known lung disease, typically young, tall, thin men. Risk rises with smoking (about 22-fold in men) and a family history.
  • Secondary spontaneous: underlying lung disease, such as COPD, infection (TB, PJP), cystic fibrosis, connective tissue disease, malignancy, or catamenial pneumothorax.
  • Traumatic: blunt or penetrating trauma, rib fractures, or iatrogenic (central lines, lung biopsy, ventilation).
  • Tension: any of these can progress to tension.

The history and examination

In a breathless trauma patient, establish the mechanism and timing, characterise the pain, and screen for other injuries: head strike and loss of consciousness, neck pain, and abdominal or left shoulder-tip pain, since a fall onto the left lower ribs can injure the spleen. Ask briefly about the dangerous differentials. Tamponade is diagnosed from the signs and eFAST, not from the history. Crushing or radiating pain suggests ACS, and tearing back pain suggests dissection. Clot risk factors point to PE, cough and fever to pneumonia, and wheeze to asthma. Pain worse on pressing and moving suggests a rib fracture.

A simple pneumothorax gives sudden breathlessness and sharp one-sided pleuritic pain, with reduced expansion, hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds on that side. Tension adds tachycardia, hypoxia, hypotension, distended neck veins, absent or markedly reduced breath sounds, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side, which is a late sign.

Telling tension from its mimics at the bedside

  • Cardiac tamponade: also gives distended neck veins, hypotension and tachycardia after chest trauma (Beck's triad includes muffled heart sounds). The trachea is central and the chest resonant with equal breath sounds.
  • Haemothorax: reduced breath sounds and shock, but the side is dull to percussion and the neck veins are usually flat from blood loss.
  • Rib fractures and contusion: tenderness and pleuritic pain, but no shift and no shock alone. A chest X-ray often misses rib fractures.

Investigations

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. In suspected tension, decompress before any imaging. Bob's film was taken at 09:48, while his BP was still maintained. It already showed complete collapse and mediastinal shift, but no one had looked at it. The diagnosis must be made at the bedside, not from the film. The film also shows a hyperexpanded left hemithorax with a depressed, flattened left hemidiaphragm and widened intercostal spaces, and no effusion to suggest a haemothorax. In a stable patient, an erect PA chest X-ray shows a visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it. In trauma, ultrasound (eFAST) detects pneumothorax, haemothorax and pericardial fluid at the bedside, and CT helps define the cause and other injuries once the patient is stable. Bloods include FBC, coagulation (reassuring for the intercostal catheter, which would not be delayed for results), and group and hold. A gas and an ECG complete the work-up.

On the NSW adult chart, his triage RR and SpO2 were in the yellow zone (clinical review). The repeat set had a red-zone systolic BP (rapid response), so a senior doctor needed to be at the bedside at once.

Management

  1. Escalate and support: resus bay, senior ED doctor and trauma team, ABCDE primary survey, high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask, monitoring and IV access.
  2. Immediate decompression on the affected side: a needle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line (preferred in adults in ATLS), or the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line. Finger thoracostomy by a trained clinician is an alternative in trauma. A needle may fail in a muscular chest wall, so reassess straight after.
  3. Intercostal catheter: after decompression, insert a chest drain in the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the safe triangle (the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, and a line at the level of the nipple, with the apex below the axilla). Use an aseptic technique and connect it to an underwater seal drain. Repeat the chest X-ray to check the tube position and re-expansion.
  4. Analgesia: titrated IV opioid in small increments with care given hypotension (e.g. fentanyl 0.5 microgram/kg, about 25–50 microgram, repeated to effect), plus regular paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly (max 4 g/day). Good analgesia also lets him breathe deeply and cough with the rib injury.
  5. Other injuries and disposition: secondary survey and eFAST; wound care and tetanus status for his grazes (give tetanus vaccine ± immunoglobulin per the Australian Immunisation Handbook); then admission under the trauma or surgical team.

For comparison, eTG manages a primary spontaneous pneumothorax with analgesia, oxygen if hypoxaemic and a period of observation (about 4 hours), with discharge if stable plus return advice and review until resolved. Aspiration or an intercostal catheter is used if the patient is symptomatic or unstable. A secondary spontaneous pneumothorax is admitted; most need aspiration or an intercostal catheter unless it is very small and the patient has few symptoms. Smoking cessation is advised, and pleurodesis is considered for recurrence. Complications of pneumothorax include tension, recurrence, respiratory failure, haemopneumothorax and pneumomediastinum.

Safety netting and follow-up

Before discharge, Bob should know to call 000 or come straight to the ED for sudden or worsening breathlessness, new or worse chest pain or feeling faint. He should not fly until a follow-up X-ray confirms full resolution and then for about 2 more weeks (confirm with the treating team). He should not mountain bike or play football until cleared, and before any scuba diving he needs a diving medical assessment with a SPUMS-trained doctor. A traumatic pneumothorax that has fully healed has a low recurrence risk, unlike a spontaneous one, and not smoking or vaping lowers the risk further. Follow-up is a clinic review with a repeat chest X-ray, and a discharge letter to his GP.
points: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: breathlessness, hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and hyper-resonance with reduced or absent breath sounds. Decompress before imaging.

Decompress at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line (or the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line), or by finger thoracostomy, then insert an intercostal catheter in the safe triangle on an underwater seal.

After chest trauma, distended neck veins with hypotension can be tension or tamponade: tracheal deviation, hyper-resonance and one-sided breath sounds point to tension. A dull hemithorax with flat neck veins points to haemothorax.

Read a pneumothorax film systematically: identifiers and RIPE, the visceral pleural edge with no markings beyond, mediastinal shift and a depressed hemidiaphragm (the deep sulcus sign is the supine-film equivalent). A normal-looking film does not exclude a rib fracture.
Act on the chart: a red-zone systolic BP calls for a rapid response, and a patient worsening between sets needs a senior doctor at the bedside now.

In every breathless trauma patient, screen for other injuries (head, neck, spleen). Safety-net with 000 for recurrent breathlessness or chest pain, no flying or contact sport until cleared, and follow-up with a repeat X-ray.
